prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Two floors up, at the corner of Hearst and Shattuck, he’s clamped for good in an iron lung. When it’s time to eat he nudges his head a sweaty mile to the edge of the pillow. It takes a while. His brilliant bloodshot light-blue eyes steer me from cupboard to fridge: he would like his chicken burrito cut into bite-size pieces, a bent straw for his glass of water, please. How does the body live its only life in a cage? I watch him compute the distance from bar to bar, and squeeze between them with a violent compression, a fury of bursting free that doesn’t last. His will is a crowbar, angled to pry up the rooted intractable weight of matter. I watch him slyly, I check out the way he does it. He does it. But pain in its absolute privacy weighs what it weighs. I come here to study the soul, posing one question a dozen ways, most of them silent. “If I’m only a body,” he laughs, “I’m up shit creek.” His laugh a gritty eruption of rock, salt and breath. Like me he writes poems but he does it letter by letter on a propped keyboard, the mouth-stick wobbling between his teeth. That kind of speed keeps a poet accountable. He won’t ever say, “The grass is very green” when it’s only green.

outputs.L2:
Two stories above the intersection of Hearst and Shattuck, he is permanently confined to an iron lung. At mealtime, he inches his head across what must feel like a perspiration-soaked mile until he reaches the pillow’s edge. The effort is slow. With striking, bloodshot, pale-blue eyes, he directs me from the cabinet to the refrigerator: he wants his chicken burrito divided into small bites and asks for a curved straw in his water glass. How can a body experience its single lifetime while imprisoned? I see him measure the gaps between the bars, then force himself through them by an intense act of contraction—a brief, furious escape. His determination works like a lever trying to lift the stubborn, deeply anchored mass of the physical world. I observe discreetly, studying how he manages. And he does manage. Yet suffering, sealed inside the person who feels it, retains its full burden.

I visit to investigate the soul, asking the same question in twelve different forms, usually without speaking. Laughing, he says, “If I’m nothing but a body, I’m in deep shit.” The sound comes out rough and explosive, made of stone, salt, and air. He writes poetry, as I do, though he composes one character at a time on a raised keyboard, guiding a mouth-stick that trembles between his teeth. Writing at such a pace forces precision. He would never claim that “the grass is exceptionally green” if it is merely green.
outputs.L3:
Confined to an iron lung, the man depends on painstaking movements of his head and the help of others for even the simplest acts of eating and drinking. Every gesture requires concentration, patience, and trust. Yet his fierce will continually pushes against the limits of his body and the private pain those limits impose.

The narrator visits him not merely to witness the practical realities of his life, but also to understand the source of his resilience. Their encounter raises larger questions about identity, dignity, and the nature of the soul: if the body is severely restricted, where does freedom reside? The man approaches such questions with humor, using wit to resist pity and to reject the notion that human existence can be reduced to physical ability alone.

His poetry offers the clearest expression of that resistance. Holding a stick in his mouth, he types each poem letter by letter. The work is extraordinarily slow and demands exact control, since every word carries the weight of sustained effort. This method leaves little room for carelessness. Through precision, patience, and honesty, he transforms physical confinement into creative expression, demonstrating that imagination and spirit can remain powerful even when the body is profoundly limited.
outputs.L4:
The narrator observes a poet whose life is largely confined to an iron lung. The machine that keeps him alive also defines the physical limits of his world: every movement is difficult, every interruption matters, and even the simplest task demands planning and endurance. Yet the poet refuses to let the machinery become the whole meaning of his existence. Through conversation, humor, study, and writing, he creates an inner life far larger than the narrow space occupied by his body.

Living with constant dependence has made him acutely aware of the relationship between body and will. Pain and weakness cannot be ignored, but neither do they completely govern him. He responds to discomfort with patience, irritation, wit, and, above all, persistence. His jokes are not merely a way of distracting himself from suffering. They allow him to retain control over how others see him and how he understands his own condition. By laughing at awkward situations and acknowledging the absurdities of daily life, he resists being reduced to an object of pity.

Writing is the clearest expression of this resistance. Because he cannot use his hands, he composes with a stick held in his mouth, pressing one key at a time. The process is exhausting and painfully slow. Each word requires physical effort, and each revision demands a degree of concentration that most writers never have to consider. What appears effortless on the page is therefore the result of extraordinary discipline. A line of poetry may represent hours of labor, repeated adjustments, and careful decisions about rhythm, sound, and meaning.

This painstaking method shapes the poet’s creative process. He cannot afford to treat language casually. Every word must justify the effort needed to type it. He listens closely to the weight of syllables and the movement of a sentence, testing whether an image is precise enough or a phrase is honest enough to remain. His physical limitations do not lessen his artistic standards; instead, they make those standards more exacting. He revises not simply to polish his work but to discover the truest possible form of what he wants to say.

As the narrator watches him, the poet’s struggle becomes more than a story of disability or survival. It becomes an inquiry into how body, pain, will, and soul coexist. The body may impose severe boundaries, but consciousness continues to question, imagine, remember, and create. Pain may narrow attention, yet it can also intensify perception. The will cannot erase physical reality, but it can decide how to meet that reality. The soul—understood as the deepest center of identity—appears not as something separate from suffering, but as something revealed through the struggle to give suffering meaning.

The poet’s persistence is fierce, though never simple or sentimental. He experiences frustration, exhaustion, and doubt. His courage does not consist in remaining cheerful at all times, nor does his art transform hardship into an easy lesson. Instead, his resilience lies in returning to the work despite discouragement. He continues to study, to joke, to argue, and to revise. Each act affirms that his life contains more than illness and that his voice deserves the same seriousness as any other writer’s.

Gradually, the narrator comes to understand that confinement and freedom are not absolute opposites. The poet’s body is restricted in the most literal sense, but his imagination remains active and expansive. His dependence on machines and other people does not eliminate independence of thought. Indeed, the severe limits placed upon him seem to sharpen his awareness of choice: the choice to speak honestly, to shape experience into art, and to refuse silence.

His poetry therefore emerges as evidence of freedom exercised under pressure. It does not deny the iron lung, the pain, or the daily humiliations of dependence. Rather, it transforms them into language without allowing them to define the whole person. Through exacting craft and relentless effort, the poet proves that physical confinement need not extinguish creativity. It may instead concentrate the mind, strengthen resilience, and produce a poetic truth grounded in the most difficult realities of human existence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about visiting a severely disabled poet who lives in an iron lung, focusing on the body, pain, freedom, and the painstaking act of writing with a mouth-stick.
counterfactuals.output:
The room is arranged around his breathing.

At its center, the iron lung—long, pale, tidal—holds his body as the sea holds a drowned bell, not silencing it, but giving it another element in which to ring. The machine sighs him open, gathers him closed. Each breath arrives by labor, by metal, by an old agreement between pressure and flesh.

Only his head is outside.

He smiles, and the room changes allegiance.

Pain lives here, but not as a monarch. It is a weather that enters without knocking, a dark pressure behind the eyes, a spark traveling the ruined roads of the nerves. He does not praise it. He does not call it teacher. He lets it be what it is: the nail, the flame, the animal that will not sleep.

Above his face hangs the mouth-stick.

He takes it between his teeth with the care of someone lifting a match in wind. At the far end, a pencil, a key, a small instrument of trespass. His neck trembles. The stick travels toward the page one fraction at a time. A letter appears.

Then another.

The labor is almost invisible: jaw, breath, patience; the body narrowed to a single deliberate point. I think of all the careless words I have thrown into the world, whole fistfuls, never feeling their weight. Here, each syllable must cross a distance. Each comma costs muscle. Each line is carried out of the body as if through fire.

Yet he is not trapped inside the sentence.

He enters it.

On the page he stands, runs, kneels beside rivers. He climbs the blue scaffolding of morning. He touches another person without permission from gravity. Freedom is not the absence of the machine, he tells me, but the presence of a door—and language, painstaking language, is one door.

The iron lung exhales.

The pencil taps.

Outside, people hurry past in their temporary bodies, mistaking motion for liberty. Inside, a man barely moving makes a field, a road, a sky large enough for both of us.

When I leave, he is still writing.

His mouth closes around the narrow wand. His eyes fix on the blankness ahead. The machine breathes. Pain waits. The page receives the slow black marks—

not footsteps exactly,

but something that travels farther.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a vivid first-person literary scene in which the narrator feeds a paralyzed friend in Berkeley and quietly studies how his fierce intelligence transcends his physical confinement.
counterfactuals.output:
Fog pressed its pale thumb against the Berkeley windows, blurring the eucalyptus beyond the glass. From the kitchen came the ticking of the old radiator and the faint, medicinal sweetness of pears simmered with ginger.

I held the spoon near Daniel’s mouth.

“Ready?”

His eyes moved once toward mine: yes.

He could still swallow if we were patient. Everything required patience now—the towel tucked beneath his chin, the careful angle of his headrest, the half-second pause after each bite. His body lay quiet in the wheelchair, hands curled uselessly in his lap, but his gaze had lost none of its old velocity. It leapt from the spoon to the rain stippling the window, to the book open on the table between us, to me.

I fed him a small mouthful. He closed his lips around the spoon, and I drew it away.

On the table was a battered copy of Spinoza, crowded with Daniel’s notes from years before his illness. The margins bristled with objections. *Too easy,* one said. *Define freedom.* Another: *The body is not a prison unless the mind agrees to be a jailer.*

I had read that sentence three times since arriving.

“Show-off,” I murmured.

His eyes sharpened with amusement.

We had devised an alphabet from glances: up for the first row, down for the second; blink to choose, wait to continue. It was laborious, absurdly so, but Daniel wielded it like a rapier. After the next spoonful, he began.

C.

O.

W.

A.

R.

D.

I laughed. “I’m a coward?”

Blink.

“For calling you a show-off?”

No.

“For not arguing with Spinoza?”

Blink.

Outside, a bus sighed at the corner, releasing students in bright waterproof jackets. Their voices rose through the wet air—careless, urgent, alive with deadlines. Daniel listened. For one moment his face seemed emptied of expression, and I feared I had mistaken endurance for peace.

Then his eyes returned to the book.

Again he spelled.

F.

R.

E.

E.

D.

O.

M.

I waited.

I.

S.

A.

V.

E.

R.

B.

The room went still around the sentence.

I looked at him—at the stubborn flame in his eyes, at the body that would not lift a finger, at the mind still rearranging the world into propositions sharp enough to cut us both free. He had not escaped his confinement; that would have been a sentimental lie. He inhabited every inch of it. He measured it, mocked it, argued with it. He made of its walls a blackboard.

I lifted another spoonful of pear.

Daniel glanced toward the window, where the fog had begun to thin above the rooftops. A strip of late sunlight lay across the floor, narrow and gold.

“Ready?” I asked.

His eyes met mine.

Yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a paragraph of poetic nonfiction exploring the question “How does the body live its only life in a cage?” Include concrete details such as a chicken burrito, a bent straw, bloodshot blue eyes, and a keyboard operated letter by letter.
counterfactuals.output: How does the body live its only life in a cage? It learns the dimensions by bruise and repetition, shoulder to wall, knee to steel, the narrow bunk holding each night like a held breath. It eats a chicken burrito gone cold at the edges, drinks through a bent straw, and watches the guard’s bloodshot blue eyes avoid its own. Still, the body insists: the pulse taps its contraband message; the lungs lift and lower their small gates; one stubborn hand approaches a keyboard operated letter by letter, pressing each key as if opening a window. Outside, rain darkens the pavement, birds quarrel on a wire, and someone who is free wastes an hour without knowing its price. Inside, the body makes a country of inches, living not beyond the cage but fiercely within it, where even hunger, pain, and longing become proof that the locked thing has not vanished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense, image-rich character portrait of an iron-lung patient whose humor and dedication to poetry remain undiminished. Contrast the weight of matter with the force of human will.
counterfactuals.output:
The iron lung fills the room like a grounded torpedo, all rivets, enamel, and blunt mechanical faith. Its steel cylinder holds the weight of the world: pistons, pressure gauges, rubber seals, the cold arithmetic of breath. Inside it, his body lies nearly motionless, pinned beneath gravity as if matter itself has issued a verdict.

Only his head emerges.

And what a defiant country it is.

His hair flares against the white collar; his eyes are quick with weather. A pencil rests near his mouth, ready to be gripped between his teeth. Above him, a mirror tilts the room into view—doorway, ceiling, visitors, the scrap of sky allowed by the window. He surveys this inverted kingdom with the expression of a man who has caught the universe making an obvious mistake.

“Luxury accommodation,” he says, glancing at the hulking machine. “Private room. Excellent ventilation.”

The iron lung answers with its steady animal rhythm: hush-thump, hush-thump. Each cycle draws air into him, then releases it, patient as a blacksmith’s bellows. The sound should be oppressive. Instead, he uses it as meter. It becomes the footfall beneath a line, the dark drum under the bright wire of language.

He writes slowly. Every word must cross a wilderness of effort: thought to jaw, jaw to pencil, pencil to page. There is no careless sentence. A comma costs him. A revision is an expedition. Yet the poems arrive sharp and alive—orchards burning red in October, rain needling the river, a woman laughing under a station clock. His body cannot turn toward the world, so he turns the world toward him, hauling it in by image, rhythm, memory.

Matter has mass. Steel weighs hundreds of pounds. Bone can fail. Muscle can fall silent. The chest can become a locked room requiring machinery to open and close its door.

But will has no measurable weight.

It slips through every seam.

His jokes flash like contraband. His poems bloom where no soil was promised. Nurses enter weary and leave laughing; visitors come prepared to offer comfort and discover themselves consoled. He refuses the solemnity others try to drape over him. Pity, in his presence, looks clumsy and overdressed.

At night, the machine labors on, moonlight glazing its curved shell. He lies within it like a letter sealed in metal, still being written. The room contracts to pressure, breath, and the faint scratch of pencil. Outside, cars pass, trees bend, whole crowds hurry through their unexamined freedom.

Inside, a man who cannot lift his hand raises cathedrals.

The iron lung keeps his body breathing.

The poems prove that breathing is not the same as being alive—and that even under the immense weight of matter, the human spirit can remain astonishingly, almost insolently, uncrushed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a prose-poetry passage about a poet trapped in an immobilized body, ending with the idea that writing so slowly forces him to choose every word honestly and precisely.
counterfactuals.output:
The poet lies beneath the white patience of the ceiling, his body a country sealed by snow. Around him, machines blink their small green constellations; a curtain breathes when the door opens. He cannot lift a hand to catch the morning, cannot turn his face from the rain’s gray handwriting on the window. Yet inside, language keeps moving—fox-quick, river-bright—crowding the narrow gate of his mouth.

A nurse holds the alphabet before him. She follows his eyes: row by row, letter by letter. A blink means yes. A pause means begin again. Hours gather around a single sentence. Afternoon darkens before he finds the noun he wants; night arrives while he searches for its truest verb.

Once, words came to him in flocks. Now each one must cross alone.

He discovers their hidden weights: grief is heavier than sorrow; blue is sometimes too easy; love, if it is to remain, must be stripped of decoration. He cannot afford the pretty lie, the careless rhythm, the word chosen merely because it was near. Writing so slowly forces him to choose every word honestly and precisely.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
